title: Sewing a zip into a crochet piece
subtitle: Inserting a zip into a bag, purse, or cardigan neckline by hand
excerpt: Sewing a zip into crochet fabric requires a different approach from sewing into woven fabric. The stretchy, open structure of crochet needs to be stabilised before the zip tape is attached, otherwise the zip pulls and distorts the opening each time it is used.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins). Contemporary garment-making and crochet finishing references.

glossaryTerms.definition: The woven fabric strip along each side of a zip, through which the zip is sewn to the garment. The teeth or coil run along the centre of the tape.

A hand sewing stitch worked by pushing the needle straight down through all layers and then straight back up, rather than scooping the needle in one motion. Gives precise control on thick or uneven surfaces.

content.text: Sewing a zip into crochet requires stabilising the opening first. Crochet fabric stretches; a zip does not. If the
is sewn directly to unstabilised crochet, the opening will distort under the tension of the zip teeth and the stitches nearest the zip will be pulled out of shape in use.

The solution is a facing: a row or two of tight double crochet (UK) worked along the opening edge to create a firm, stable strip that the zip tape can be pinned and stitched to. The zip attaches to the facing, not to the open crochet fabric behind it.

items.name: Zip, correct length for the opening
items.note: Buy a zip 1 to 2 cm shorter than the opening, not the same length. A zip that reaches the full length of the opening forces the pull to the very ends, which strains the crochet.

items.name: Sewing thread to match the zip tape colour
Hand sewing needle, sharp tip
items.note: A blunt tapestry needle will not pass through the tightly woven zip tape.

items.name: Pins
items.note: For holding the zip in position before stitching

content.text: Work a stabilising facing: pick up a row of double crochet (UK) along each side of the opening with the same yarn as the garment. Use a hook one size smaller than the body to keep the facing firm. This facing will carry the zip.
Close the zip. Lay it face-down against the wrong side of the opening, with the zip teeth running along the centre of the opening gap. The zip should be centred and short of the ends by 1 to 2 cm.
Pin the zip tape to the facing on each side, working from the centre outward. Do not stretch the crochet or the zip tape while pinning.
Sew the zip to the facing using
: push the needle straight through the zip tape and facing and pull through, then bring it back up through both layers 3 to 4 mm along. Work along the full length of each side of the tape.
Turn to the right side. The zip teeth should sit in the gap between the two facing edges, with the tape hidden behind the facing. Open and close the zip several times to test the alignment.
If the pull end of the zip protrudes beyond the crochet edge, fold the excess tape to the wrong side and sew it flat before finishing the zip ends.

items.symptom: The zip is visible from the front as a ridge along the opening
items.cause: The zip tape was sewn too close to the teeth, pushing the tape forward rather than keeping it flat behind the facing.
items.fix: Unpick and reposition the zip 2 to 3 mm further from the teeth. The tape should sit well inside the facing, with only the teeth visible through the gap.

items.symptom: The crochet is puckering around the zip
items.cause: The facing was pulled too tight while the zip was being pinned, or the stabbing stitches are too close together and gathering the facing.
items.fix: Ease out any puckering by loosening the stitches and redistributing them. Sew with larger stitches further from the zip edge.

items.symptom: The zip pull is hard to move once the zip is installed
items.cause: The gap between the two facing edges is too narrow, causing the teeth to bind when the pull is operated.
items.fix: Ease one facing edge away from the other by a millimetre or two using the crochet hook to pull the outermost stitches outward. The teeth need a clear channel.

content.text: A small zip-top pouch is the standard first zip insertion project: a rectangular flat piece folded in half and seamed at the sides, with a short zip along the top opening. At this scale the seam is short enough to unpick and redo without ruining the project if the first attempt is not quite right.
